```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", dev = "png",
                      fig.retina = 2, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.4,
                      fig.align = "center")
library(mlvtoolbox)
# Panels drawn by plot() on an mlv_mat need little margin; knitr resets par()
# after every chunk, so this hook affects only the chunks that request it.
knitr::knit_hooks$set(tight = function(before, options, envir)
  if (before) par(mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 0.5), cex.main = 1, font.main = 1))
okabe <- c(blue = "#0072B2", orange = "#E69F00", green = "#009E73",
           vermillion = "#D55E00", sky = "#56B4E9")
```

Contour measurements describe each stroke on its own. The medial-axis
measurements describe the *space between* strokes: whether two contours run
parallel, how far apart they are, whether they mirror each other, and whether
the gap between them narrows at a constant rate. `mlvtoolbox` computes four
such *branch scores* (parallelism, separation, mirror and taper) from the
medial axis of a rasterized drawing, following Walther et al. (2023) and
Rezanejad et al. (2019), and maps them back onto the contour pixels.

The computation has five stages, each stored in the `mlv_mat` object that
`compute_mat()` returns:

1. rasterize the drawing into ink pixels;
2. compute a signed *distance map* to the ink;
3. compute the *average outward flux* (AOF, "flux") of that distance map;
4. threshold the flux and thin the result to a one-pixel *skeleton*;
5. trace the skeleton into ordered *branches*, each point carrying a radius.

`compute_mat_properties()` then scores every branch point, and
`map_mat_properties()` transfers the scores to the contours. This vignette
follows one small drawing through every stage with `plot()` on the `mlv_mat`,
then explains each score with a pair of drawings that differ in only that
respect. All values come from the package defaults;
`vignette("mlv-compatibility", package = "mlvtoolbox")` shows how to reproduce
values published with the MATLAB toolbox.

## The running example

The drawing has three contours on an 80 by 50 pixel canvas: a straight line
at y = 18, a second line below it that runs from y = 32 to y = 30, so the gap
narrows slightly from left to right, and a shallow open V beneath both.

```{r example}
seg <- function(...) matrix(c(...), nrow = 1)
drawing <- mlv_drawing(list(
  seg(10, 18, 70, 18),
  seg(10, 32, 70, 30),
  rbind(c(20, 40, 40, 44), c(40, 44, 60, 40))), width = 80, height = 50)
mat <- compute_mat(drawing)
mat
```

`compute_mat()` accepts a drawing or a logical ink matrix. Given a drawing,
it first calls `rasterize()` with a line width of one pixel.

```{r stage-ink, tight = TRUE, fig.height = 2.9, fig.cap = "Stage 1. Rasterized ink (black) under the vector contours (orange). The enlargement (right) shows the dashed box on its pixel grid: each segment becomes one pixel per step along its longer axis, so a 2-pixel rise over 60 pixels becomes three flat runs joined by one-pixel steps."}
layout(matrix(1:2, 1), widths = c(1.45, 1))
plot(mat, "ink", drawing = drawing, overlay_col = okabe[["vermillion"]],
     overlay_lwd = 1.5, legend = FALSE, main = "1  Ink")
rect(12.5, 28.5, 30.5, 34.5, border = "grey40", lty = 2)
plot(mat, "ink", drawing = drawing, overlay_col = okabe[["vermillion"]],
     overlay_lwd = 1.5, legend = FALSE, grid = TRUE, xlim = c(12.5, 30.5),
     ylim = c(28.5, 34.5), main = "Enlarged")
```

## Signed distance map

The distance map gives, for every pixel, the Euclidean distance in pixels to
the nearest ink pixel. `compute_mat()` first thins the ink to strokes one
pixel wide, so a thick stroke is measured from its centre line. Ink pixels
then have distance 0, except an isolated single ink pixel, which has −1; that
negative value is why the map is called signed. Only ink counts as boundary:
the canvas edge is not a contour, so the distance keeps growing towards the
corners.

```{r stage-distance, tight = TRUE, fig.height = 3.95, fig.cap = sprintf("Stage 2. Distance from each pixel to the nearest ink pixel, with isolines every 2 px. Where the isolines from two contours meet they fold into creases; these ridges, halfway between neighbouring contours, are the medial axis that the later stages extract. The corners are darkest only because the canvas edge is not a boundary. The map is called signed, but this drawing has no isolated single ink pixel, so its smallest value is %g and no pixel is negative.", min(mat$distance_map))}
plot(mat, "distance", levels = seq(2, 22, by = 2),
     main = "2  Distance to ink")
```

```{r distance-range}
range(mat$distance_map[mat$mask])     # on ink
max(mat$distance_map)                 # farthest pixel from any ink, in px
```

## Average outward flux

Away from the ink the distance map rises at the same rate in every
direction; a ridge is where the slopes rising from two different contours
meet. The flux detects that meeting. Around each pixel the method places a circle of radius `epsilon`
(1 pixel) and takes `samples` (60) evenly spaced points on it. At each point
it forms the unit vector towards that point's nearest ink pixel (averaged
over equally near ink pixels) and takes the dot product with the circle's
outward normal. The stored value is the sum of
the 60 dot products.

On the medial axis, the points on either side of the circle have their nearest
ink on their own side, so their vectors point outwards and the sum is large
and positive. On and next to ink, the vectors point back across the circle and
the sum is negative. For a point midway between two parallel straight
boundaries, the continuous average is 2/π per sample, which is
`r round(60 * 2 / pi, 1)` for 60 samples; on the pixel grid the sum is
somewhat lower.

```{r stage-flux, tight = TRUE, fig.height = 3.95, fig.cap = sprintf("Stage 3. Outward flux, stored as the sum over %d sample points. Positive flux (red) forms ridges midway between contours; negative flux (blue) hugs the ink. The dashed line encloses the pixels above the skeleton threshold, %.1f, also marked on the colour bar. Above the middle of the top line nearly every sample's nearest ink lies straight below it, so the vectors almost cancel and the flux is close to zero (%.1f to %.1f, near-white).", mat$parameters$samples, mat$parameters$threshold * mat$parameters$samples, min(mat$AOF[2:16, 15:65]), max(mat$AOF[2:16, 15:65]))}
plot(mat, "flux", drawing = drawing, main = "3  Outward flux")
```

Pixels whose sampling circle would leave the canvas are set to zero, which is
why a one-pixel frame shows no flux.

## Threshold and skeleton

A pixel belongs to the medial axis if its flux exceeds
`samples * threshold`, where `threshold = (2/π) sin(threshold_angle)`. The
*object angle* `threshold_angle` (default 28°) is the angle between the axis
and the direction to the nearest boundary: for two parallel boundaries it is
90°, and at the open end of a structure, where the two sides diverge, it
shrinks towards zero. The default threshold is
`r round(mat$parameters$threshold, 4)`, so a pixel needs a flux above
`r round(mat$parameters$threshold * mat$parameters$samples, 2)`.

The thresholded region is often two or three pixels wide. `skeletonize()`
thins it to a one-pixel skeleton with the same 8-connected topology; the
default `morphology = "minimal"` leaves no pixel that could be removed without
changing that topology. Components smaller than `min_component` pixels
(default 2.5% of the larger image side) are dropped.

```{r stage-skeleton, tight = TRUE, fig.height = 3.95, fig.cap = "Stage 4. Pixels above the flux threshold (light red), thinned to a one-pixel skeleton (dark red); ink in black. Where the thresholded region is one pixel wide, the skeleton covers it completely. The skeleton runs midway between each pair of contours and continues past their open ends, where the nearest boundaries are the two contour endpoints."}
plot(mat, "skeleton", main = "4  Threshold and skeleton")
```

```{r skeleton-count}
c(above_threshold = sum(mat$AOF > mat$parameters$threshold * mat$parameters$samples),
  skeleton = sum(mat$skeleton))
```

## Branches

`trace_skeleton()`, called by `compute_mat()`, splits the skeleton into
*branches*: paths between end pixels and junction pixels. Each branch is a
data frame with one row per skeleton pixel, in path order, holding its
position and its *radius*, the distance map at that pixel. The radius is the
radius of the largest disc centred on the axis that touches ink. A junction
pixel belongs to every branch that meets there, but appears only once within
a branch.

```{r branches}
n_points <- vapply(mat$branches, nrow, integer(1))
n_points
head(mat$branches[[1]])
```

```{r stage-branches, tight = TRUE, fig.height = 3.95, fig.cap = sprintf("Stage 5. The traced branches, each coloured and labelled with its index in mat$branches. Grey circles are maximal inscribed discs at every tenth branch point: each is centred on the axis, touches the nearest ink, and has the branch radius. The two pixels inside the V form a separate component. At %d pixels it is not smaller than min_component (%g px on this canvas), and spur pruning never removes a component's last path, so it survives as branch 3.", nrow(mat$branches[[3]]), mat$parameters$min_component)}
plot(mat, "branches", discs = 10, main = "5  Branches")
```

Small irregularities in a contour give the skeleton short side branches. A
*spur* is a path from an end pixel to a junction, and spurs with fewer than
`min_branch_points` pixels (default 10, junction included) are removed. The
shortest spurs go first; after each removal, two paths that meet at a pixel
where nothing else branches are joined into one branch, so a junction that
has lost its spur no longer splits the axis. Two rules keep the result
independent of tracing order and keep small shapes measurable. Spurs of equal
length are treated alike: if removing all of a junction's shortest spurs would
leave it with fewer than two paths, all of them are kept. And only spurs are
removed, so no skeleton component loses its last path. The four equal arms of a
small square's X-shaped skeleton are therefore all kept, while a spur on a
long axis is removed.

```{r spur, tight = TRUE, fig.height = 2.1, fig.cap = "A short stub on the upper of two lines gives the skeleton two 8-pixel spurs. With min_branch_points = 2 (left) the skeleton is traced as five branches; with the default, 10 (right), both spurs are removed and the axis between the lines is a single branch."}
stub <- mlv_drawing(list(seg(10, 10, 70, 10), seg(10, 30, 70, 30),
                         seg(40, 10, 40, 15)), width = 80, height = 40)
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(compute_mat(stub, min_branch_points = 2), "branches", legend = FALSE,
     main = "Spurs kept")
plot(compute_mat(stub), "branches", legend = FALSE,
     main = "Spurs removed (default)")
par(op)
```

## Branch scores

`compute_mat_properties()` scores every point of every branch. Parallelism,
separation and mirror are computed by default; taper must be requested.

```{r scores}
mat <- compute_mat_properties(
  mat, properties = c("parallelism", "separation", "mirror", "taper"))
round(sapply(c("parallelism", "separation", "mirror", "taper"),
             function(p) sapply(mat$branches, function(b) median(b[[p]]))), 3)
```

The table gives the median over each branch's points. All four scores lie
between 0 and 1, and all four end in the same two steps: a moving mean over
three neighbouring points, then a power of 10 (`power`), which spreads the
values near 1. Under the default `branch_rule = "invariant"`, each score is
the mean of the scores computed in the two traversal directions, so it does
not depend on which end the tracer started from.

Some points have no score. Parallelism and taper compare a point's
neighbours on both sides, so the two end points of a branch, and every point
of a branch with fewer than three points, are undefined; mirror needs more
than three points; separation is undefined below radius 1. The default marks
these points NA, and the moving mean averages only the defined values around
each point, so a branch end takes the value of its defined neighbour (that
point's value before smoothing) instead of being pulled towards zero. A value
of exactly 0 is defined and is averaged like any other. The two-pixel branch 3 has no interior point, so its
parallelism, mirror and taper are NA (the median above is NA); its
separation is defined. The published estimator (`branch_rule = "mlv2023"`)
scores undefined points 0 and averages those zeros into their neighbours.

```{r stage-scores, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = sprintf("Branch scores plotted under the branches they belong to, against image x. Parallelism is near 1 along the middle of the upper channel (branch 1) and falls past both open ends, where the axis leaves the channel and its radius grows. Separation (note the axis, 0 to 0.5) is higher along branch 1 (median %.2f) than along branch 2 (median %.2f), whose gap is narrower, and rises at the open ends with the radius. Branch 3 has two points, both at x = %d: it has no parallelism, and its separation appears as a dot.", median(mat$branches[[1]]$separation), median(mat$branches[[2]]$separation), mat$branches[[3]]$x[1])}
plot_branch_profile(mat, c("parallelism", "separation"),
                    ylim = list(separation = c(0, 0.5)))
```

Each score is easiest to understand on two drawings that differ in only the
property it measures. The helper below computes the scores and returns the
branch with the most points, sorted from left to right.

```{r helper}
poly <- function(x, y) cbind(head(x, -1), head(y, -1), x[-1], y[-1])
P <- c("parallelism", "separation", "mirror", "taper")
score_pair <- function(d) compute_mat_properties(compute_mat(d), properties = P)
main_branch <- function(m) {
  b <- m$branches[[which.max(vapply(m$branches, nrow, integer(1)))]]
  b[order(b$x), ]
}
interior <- function(b) b$x >= 25 & b$x <= 65   # away from the open ends
```

### Parallelism

Parallelism asks whether the radius stays constant along the axis. At each
point `i`, over a window of `window` (5) points on either side, it divides the
length of the axis by the length of the curve traced by the axis together
with the radius:

parallelism(i) = Σ |Δaxis| / Σ √(|Δaxis|² + ΔR²).

A constant radius gives exactly 1. Two straight lines that converge at
half-angle θ about a horizontal axis have a radius that changes by sin θ per
pixel of axis, so before the final smoothing every point scores
1/√(1 + sin²θ), and after the power of 10, (1 + sin²θ)^−5.

```{r parallelism}
parallel <- mlv_drawing(list(poly(c(10, 80), c(15, 15)),
                             poly(c(10, 80), c(35, 35))), 90, 50)
converging <- mlv_drawing(list(poly(c(10, 80), c(8, 22)),
                               poly(c(10, 80), c(42, 28))), 90, 50)
m_par <- score_pair(parallel); m_con <- score_pair(converging)
b_par <- main_branch(m_par); b_con <- main_branch(m_con)
theta <- atan(14 / 70)                   # each line rises 14 px over 70 px
c(parallel = median(b_par$parallelism[interior(b_par)]),
  converging = median(b_con$parallelism[interior(b_con)]),
  converging_analytical = (1 + sin(theta)^2)^-5)
```

```{r fig-parallelism, fig.height = 4.6, fig.cap = sprintf("Parallelism along the axis of two parallel lines (left) and of two lines converging at %.1f° each (right). Discs show the radius at every tenth axis point; the shaded band is the interior (x 25 to 65) over which the medians are taken. Constant width keeps the radius flat and scores 1; steady narrowing lowers parallelism along the channel to a median of %.2f. Both fall where the axis leaves through an open end. Near the apex of the converging pair (x ≥ 78), where the raster radius stops changing (%.1f to %.1f px), parallelism rises again, to %.2f.", theta * 180 / pi, median(b_con$parallelism[interior(b_con)]), min(b_con$radius[b_con$x >= 78]), max(b_con$radius[b_con$x >= 78]), max(b_con$parallelism[b_con$x >= 78]))}
cols <- unname(okabe[c("blue", "orange", "green")])
show_median <- function(branches, v) function(column, row) if (row == v) {
  b <- branches[[column]]
  m <- median(b[[v]][interior(b)])
  text(45, if (m > 0.5) m - 0.22 else m + 0.22, sprintf("median %.2f", m),
       cex = 0.75, col = "grey20")
}
plot_branch_profile(list(Parallel = m_par, Converging = m_con),
                    c("radius", "parallelism"), branches = "longest", discs = 10,
                    col = cols[1:2], band = c(25, 65),
                    panel = show_median(list(b_par, b_con), "parallelism"))
```

The measured median for the converging pair,
`r round(median(b_con$parallelism[interior(b_con)]), 3)`, is a little below
the analytical `r round((1 + sin(theta)^2)^-5, 3)`. The difference comes from
the raster: the radius is a distance between pixel centres, so along a sloped
line it changes in uneven steps, and every uneven step lengthens the
denominator. Replacing the raster radius by the exact distance to the lines
recovers the analytical value:

```{r parallelism-smooth}
exact <- b_con
exact$radius <- (34 - 2 * (14 / 70) * (exact$x - 10)) / 2 * cos(theta)
both <- (score_branch(exact, "parallelism") +
         rev(score_branch(exact[nrow(exact):1, ], "parallelism"))) / 2
median(both[interior(exact)])
```

### Separation

Separation depends only on the radius R, in pixels:
separation = (1 − 1/R)^10, smoothed as above. It increases with the gap
between the contours and approaches 1 slowly: R = 3 gives
`r signif((1 - 1/3)^10, 3)`, R = 10 gives `r signif((1 - 1/10)^10, 3)` and
R = 50 gives `r signif((1 - 1/50)^10, 3)`. It is undefined (NA) below R = 1.
Because R is measured in pixels, the same drawing rendered at a higher
resolution scores higher.

```{r separation}
narrow <- mlv_drawing(list(poly(c(10, 80), c(22, 22)),
                           poly(c(10, 80), c(28, 28))), 90, 50)
wide <- mlv_drawing(list(poly(c(10, 80), c(15, 15)),
                         poly(c(10, 80), c(35, 35))), 90, 50)
m_nar <- score_pair(narrow); m_wid <- score_pair(wide)
b_nar <- main_branch(m_nar); b_wid <- main_branch(m_wid)
rbind(radius = c(narrow = median(b_nar$radius[interior(b_nar)]),
                 wide = median(b_wid$radius[interior(b_wid)])),
      separation = c(median(b_nar$separation[interior(b_nar)]),
                     median(b_wid$separation[interior(b_wid)])),
      analytical = c((1 - 1/3)^10, (1 - 1/10)^10))
```

```{r fig-separation, fig.height = 4.6, fig.cap = sprintf("Separation for a 6 px gap (left, radius %g) and a 20 px gap (right, radius %g), with discs at every tenth axis point. The score rises with the radius, from a median of %.2f to %.2f: high separation means far apart. It rises further past the open ends, where the radius grows.", median(b_nar$radius[interior(b_nar)]), median(b_wid$radius[interior(b_wid)]), median(b_nar$separation[interior(b_nar)]), median(b_wid$separation[interior(b_wid)]))}
plot_branch_profile(list("Narrow gap" = m_nar, "Wide gap" = m_wid),
                    c("radius", "separation"), branches = "longest", discs = 10,
                    col = cols[1:2], band = c(25, 65),
                    panel = show_median(list(b_nar, b_wid), "separation"))
```

### Mirror

When two contours are mirror images of each other, their line of reflection
is part of their medial axis, so that stretch of the axis is straight. The
mirror score measures how straight the axis is. `fit_line_segments()` splits the branch
greedily into straight spans, extending each span while the mean
perpendicular distance of its interior points from the chord stays within
1 pixel. A point in a span of n points scores 1 − 1/n before smoothing and
the power of 10.

The symmetric pair below consists of two bowed contours reflected about
y = 25. The asymmetric pair keeps the upper contour and replaces the lower one
with a straight line, so the axis bends to follow the upper contour.

```{r mirror}
xs <- seq(10, 80, by = 5)
upper <- poly(xs, 6 + 0.016 * (xs - 45)^2)
symmetric <- mlv_drawing(list(upper, poly(xs, 44 - 0.016 * (xs - 45)^2)), 90, 50)
asymmetric <- mlv_drawing(list(upper, poly(c(10, 80), c(38, 38))), 90, 50)
m_sym <- score_pair(symmetric); m_asy <- score_pair(asymmetric)
b_sym <- main_branch(m_sym); b_asy <- main_branch(m_asy)
spans <- function(b) fit_line_segments(cbind(b$x, b$y))$spans
rbind(spans = c(symmetric = nrow(spans(b_sym)), asymmetric = nrow(spans(b_asy))),
      mirror = c(median(b_sym$mirror), median(b_asy$mirror)),
      parallelism = c(median(b_sym$parallelism), median(b_asy$parallelism)))
```

Under the default `branch_rule = "invariant"` the axis is fitted twice, once
traced from each end, and a point's mirror score is the mean of its scores in
the two fits. The two fits can split a bent axis differently:

```{r mirror-directions}
directions <- function(b) {     # b is sorted from left to right
  n <- nrow(b)
  reverse <- spans(b[n:1, ])
  list(spans = list(forward = spans(b), reverse = n + 1 - reverse[nrow(reverse):1, 2:1, drop = FALSE]),
       score = list(forward = score_branch(b, "mirror"),
                    reverse = rev(score_branch(b[n:1, ], "mirror"))))
}
fits <- list(directions(b_sym), directions(b_asy))
lapply(fits[[2]]$spans, function(s) s[, 2] - s[, 1] + 1)   # points per span, asymmetric
```

```{r mirror-directions-check, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal((fits[[2]]$score$forward + fits[[2]]$score$reverse) / 2,
                           b_asy$mirror)),
          nrow(fits[[2]]$spans$forward) == nrow(fits[[2]]$spans$reverse),
          nrow(fits[[1]]$spans$forward) == 1L, nrow(fits[[1]]$spans$reverse) == 1L,
          length(unique(round(b_sym$mirror, 6))) == 1L,
          min(diff(fits[[2]]$spans$forward[nrow(fits[[2]]$spans$forward), ])) + 1 == 2,
          diff(fits[[2]]$spans$reverse[1, ]) + 1 == 2)
```

```{r fig-mirror, fig.height = 3.9, fig.cap = sprintf("Mirror scores along the axis. Chords show the straight spans that fit_line_segments() finds when the axis is traced left to right (blue, drawn 4 px above the axis) and right to left (orange, 4 px below), labelled with their number of points; a point in a span of n points scores 1 − 1/n before the moving mean and the power of 10. Thin lines give each fit's score; the default score (thick grey) is their mean. The symmetric pair is fitted by one %d-point span in both directions and scores %.2f everywhere. The asymmetric pair needs %d spans in each direction, so it scores lower; at each end one fit has a 2-point span, which pulls the mean down to %.2f.", nrow(b_sym), median(b_sym$mirror), nrow(fits[[2]]$spans$forward), min(b_asy$mirror))}
mirror_panel <- function(column, row) {
  b <- list(b_sym, b_asy)[[column]]; f <- fits[[column]]
  dir_col <- c(forward = okabe[["blue"]], reverse = okabe[["orange"]])
  for (k in names(dir_col)) {
    if (row == "drawing") {
      s <- f$spans[[k]]; dy <- if (k == "forward") -4 else 4
      segments(b$x[s[, 1]], b$y[s[, 1]] + dy, b$x[s[, 2]], b$y[s[, 2]] + dy,
               col = dir_col[[k]], lwd = 1.3)
      points(b$x[unique(c(s))], b$y[unique(c(s))] + dy, pch = "|", cex = 0.5,
             col = dir_col[[k]])
      long <- s[, 2] - s[, 1] >= 8
      text((b$x[s[long, 1]] + b$x[s[long, 2]]) / 2,
           (b$y[s[long, 1]] + b$y[s[long, 2]]) / 2 + 1.75 * dy,
           s[long, 2] - s[long, 1] + 1, cex = 0.6, col = dir_col[[k]])
    } else lines(b$x, f$score[[k]], col = dir_col[[k]], lwd = 1.3)
  }
}
plot_branch_profile(list("Symmetric pair" = m_sym, "Asymmetric pair" = m_asy),
                    "mirror", branches = "longest", col = "grey65", lwd = 4,
                    panel = mirror_panel)
```

The two scores dissociate. The symmetric pair has a straight axis (high
mirror) but a radius that changes along it (low parallelism); the asymmetric
pair has a bent axis but a more even gap. The mirror score also depends on
branch length: a perfectly straight branch of n points scores (1 − 1/n)^10,
which is `r signif((1 - 1/20)^10, 2)` for 20 points and
`r signif((1 - 1/80)^10, 2)` for 80 points. Compare mirror scores between
drawings whose branches have similar lengths, or summarize them over
comparable structures.

### Taper

Taper applies the parallelism formula to the change in the *rate* at which
the radius changes: the radius differences are smoothed (moving mean of
three), differenced again and smoothed again before they replace ΔR. A
constant width and a constant narrowing both score 1, so taper distinguishes a
wedge from a channel whose width changes irregularly. Taper is not in the
default `properties` and must be requested.

```{r taper}
wavy_x <- seq(10, 80, by = 2)
wave <- 4 * sin((wavy_x - 10) / 70 * 3 * pi)
wavy <- mlv_drawing(list(poly(wavy_x, 13 - wave), poly(wavy_x, 37 + wave)), 90, 50)
m_wav <- score_pair(wavy); b_wav <- main_branch(m_wav)
profiles <- list(parallel = b_par, wedge = b_con, wavy = b_wav)
round(sapply(profiles, function(b)
  c(parallelism = median(b$parallelism[interior(b)]),
    taper = median(b$taper[interior(b)]))), 3)
```

```{r fig-taper, fig.height = 5.6, fig.cap = sprintf("Three channels, their traced axes and inscribed discs (top), and, aligned below each, the radius, parallelism and taper along the axis. The wedge loses parallelism (median %.2f) but keeps taper near 1 (%.3f), because its width changes at a constant rate; the wavy channel lowers parallelism markedly (%.2f) and taper only slightly (%.3f). Medians are over the shaded interior.", median(b_con$parallelism[interior(b_con)]), median(b_con$taper[interior(b_con)]), median(b_wav$parallelism[interior(b_wav)]), median(b_wav$taper[interior(b_wav)]))}
taper_panel <- function(column, row) if (row %in% c("parallelism", "taper")) {
  b <- profiles[[column]]
  text(45, 0.2, sprintf("median %.*f", if (row == "taper") 3 else 2,
                        median(b[[row]][interior(b)])), cex = 0.75, col = "grey20")
}
plot_branch_profile(list(parallel = m_par, wedge = m_con, wavy = m_wav),
                    c("radius", "parallelism", "taper"), branches = "longest",
                    discs = 10, col = cols, band = c(25, 65), panel = taper_panel)
```

On these drawings taper stays close to 1 even for the wavy channel (median
`r round(median(b_wav$taper[interior(b_wav)]), 3)`), because the second
difference of a twice-smoothed radius is small for gradual changes.
Parallelism falls at the branch ends, where the skeleton leaves the channel
through its open ends and its radius changes rapidly. Taper stays near 1 there
as well, because the radius grows at a nearly constant rate; it measures
changes in that rate, not the rate itself.

## Mapping scores onto contours

Contour features need one score per contour pixel, not per skeleton pixel.
For every pair of consecutive branch points, `map_mat_properties()` constructs
the points where a disc rolling along the axis touches the boundary on either
side: given the two centres and their radii, these tangent points lie on the
contours if the radius was measured correctly. Each tangent point carries the
mean score of the two branch points it was built from, and each ink pixel
takes the score of its nearest tangent point, provided that point lies within
`radius` pixels (default 4). Exact distance ties and pixels reached from
several branches take the maximum score.

```{r mapping}
mapped <- map_mat_properties(drawing, mat)
names(mapped$mat_properties)
round(sapply(mapped$mat_properties$parallelism, mean, na.rm = TRUE), 3)
```

`mapped$mat_properties` holds one vector per property and contour, with one
value per contour pixel in raster order; `mapped$mat_images` holds the same
values as images, and `mapped$mat_mapping_masks` marks which ink pixels
received a score. `analyse_mat()` runs `compute_mat()`,
`compute_mat_properties()` and `map_mat_properties()` in one call.

```{r fig-mapped, tight = TRUE, fig.height = 3.95, fig.cap = "Parallelism mapped onto the contour pixels of the running example. The middle line takes the higher of the scores from the branches above and below it; at the default mapping radius every ink pixel receives a score."}
plot(mapped, property = "parallelism", axes = FALSE,
     main = "Parallelism on the contours")
```

The mapping radius trades coverage against specificity. A radius much smaller
than one pixel misses pixels where the raster radius and the vector contour
disagree by rounding; a large radius lets a branch claim pixels of a contour
that does not bound it.

```{r mapping-radius}
ink <- rasterize(drawing)
sapply(c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8), function(r) {
  z <- map_mat_properties(drawing, mat, radius = r)$mat_images$parallelism
  mean(is.finite(z[ink]))
})
```

The values are the fraction of ink pixels mapped at radii of 0.5, 1, 2, 4 and
8 pixels.

### Valid zeros and missing scores

A mapped score can be missing (NA) or a valid zero, and the two mean different
things. NA means that no branch gives the pixel a defined score: either no
branch's tangent samples lie within `radius`, or, for every branch that does,
its samples nearest to the pixel are undefined (a two-point branch has no
parallelism). Mapping does not reach past an undefined nearest sample to a
farther defined one. A single straight line has
no partner contour, so its flux never exceeds the threshold and every pixel is
NA. A 20-pixel square is fully covered: its skeleton is an X whose four tied
arms are all shorter than `min_branch_points`, and since removing them would
delete the skeleton, all four are kept.

A zero is a measurement. Two lines on rows 20 and 23 are three pixels apart,
so their geometric medial radius is 1.5 pixels. The skeleton must lie on a
pixel row, here row 21 or 22, one pixel from the nearer line, so the raster
radius is exactly 1 and the separation is (1 − 1/1)^10 = 0 at every point.
Zeros that only stand for an undefined value, such as the published scores of
a branch's end points, are NA under the default.

```{r zeros}
coverage <- function(d, ...) {
  im <- analyse_mat(d, ...)$drawing$mat_images$separation
  ink <- rasterize(d)
  c(ink = sum(ink), missing = sum(is.na(im[ink])), zero = sum(im[ink] == 0, na.rm = TRUE))
}
single <- mlv_drawing(list(poly(c(10, 50), c(20, 20))), 60, 40)
square <- mlv_drawing(list(rbind(c(10, 10, 30, 10), c(30, 10, 30, 30),
                                 c(30, 30, 10, 30), c(10, 30, 10, 10))), 40, 40)
close_pair <- mlv_drawing(list(poly(c(10, 50), c(20, 20)),
                               poly(c(10, 50), c(23, 23))), 60, 40)
rbind(single = coverage(single),
      square = coverage(square),
      close_pair = coverage(close_pair))
```

Treat missing scores as missing: exclude them from means and histograms rather
than counting them as zero. The published MATLAB code treats every zero as
missing (MLV-M011 in the
[differences register](https://github.com/bbuchsbaum/mlvtoolboxR/blob/main/DIFFERENCES.md));
`branch_rule = "mlv2023"` reproduces that, so in that mode the close pair would
have no separation values at all.

## Parameters

| Argument | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `threshold_angle` | 28° | Minimum object angle; larger values keep only points between nearly parallel boundaries. |
| `samples` | 60 | Points on the flux circle; with `aof = "centered"` it must be a multiple of 4. |
| `epsilon` | 1 px | Radius of the flux circle. |
| `min_component` | 2.5% of the larger image side | Smallest skeleton component kept, in pixels. |
| `min_branch_points` | 10 | Shortest spur kept, in pixels; a component's last path is never removed. |
| `window`, `power` | 5, 10 | Half-window (points) and exponent of the branch scores (`compute_mat_properties()`). |
| `radius` | 4 px | Maximum distance from a tangent point to a mapped ink pixel (`map_mat_properties()`). |

The multiple-of-4 rule for `samples` follows from what the default flux
guarantees: rotating or reflecting the ink raster by any of the eight
symmetries of the pixel grid rotates or reflects the flux field in the same
way. That holds only if the sample directions 2πk/`samples` map onto
themselves under a quarter turn and under reflection in the diagonal.

```{r samples-error, error = TRUE}
compute_mat(drawing, samples = 30)
```

## Where the medial axis lies

Two horizontal lines at y = 10 and y = 22 rasterize to ink rows 10 and 22.
A pixel in row r between them is r − 10 pixels from the upper line and
22 − r from the lower one, so the two distances are equal, and the distance
map has its ridge, at r = (10 + 22)/2 = 16. The medial axis should therefore
be the single row 16. The comparison below changes only the flux definition,
`aof`; the full published-compatible recipe is given in
`vignette("mlv-compatibility", package = "mlvtoolbox")`.

```{r midline}
lines2 <- mlv_drawing(list(seg(5, 10, 45, 10), seg(5, 22, 45, 22)), 50, 32)
default_flux <- compute_mat(lines2)
mlv_flux <- compute_mat(lines2, aof = "mlv2023")
cut <- default_flux$parameters$threshold * default_flux$parameters$samples
above <- function(m) which(m$AOF[, 25] > cut)   # rows above threshold in column 25
list(centered = above(default_flux), mlv2023 = above(mlv_flux))
list(centered = table(row(default_flux$skeleton)[default_flux$skeleton]),
     mlv2023 = table(row(mlv_flux$skeleton)[mlv_flux$skeleton]))
```

```{r midline-check, include = FALSE}
stopifnot(identical(above(default_flux), 16L), identical(above(mlv_flux), 16:17),
          isTRUE(all.equal(default_flux$AOF[15, 25], default_flux$AOF[17, 25])))
```

The default flux exceeds the threshold only on row 16, and its neighbours on
rows 15 and 17 have equal values. The published flux (`aof = "mlv2023"`)
exceeds it on rows 16 and 17. MATLAB's `computeAOF` centres the sampling
circle on the pixel corner, half a pixel below and to the right of the pixel
centre, but reads the nearest-boundary labels from the cell containing each
sample point, so the ridge is displaced by half a pixel and spread over two
rows (MLV-M027). Thinning removes most of the second row, but
`r sum(row(mlv_flux$skeleton)[mlv_flux$skeleton] == 17)` skeleton pixels
remain on row 17.

```{r fig-midline, fig.height = 3.4, fig.cap = sprintf("Flux down column 25, across the gap between two lines on rows 10 and 22. Filled markers exceed the threshold (dashed, %.2f); open markers do not. The default flux (blue) exceeds it only on row 16, the analytical midline; its neighbours on rows 15 and 17 are equal (%.2f) and fall just below it. The aof = \"mlv2023\" flux (orange) exceeds the threshold on rows 16 and 17.", cut, default_flux$AOF[15, 25])}
rows <- 11:21
series <- list(default = default_flux$AOF[rows, 25], mlv2023 = mlv_flux$AOF[rows, 25])
colours <- c(default = okabe[["blue"]], mlv2023 = okabe[["orange"]])
op <- par(mar = c(3.2, 3.6, 0.6, 5.6), mgp = c(2.1, 0.6, 0), las = 1, cex.axis = 0.85)
plot(NA, xlim = range(rows), ylim = range(c(unlist(series), 0)), xaxt = "n", bty = "n",
     xlab = "image row y (px)", ylab = "flux (sum of 60 samples)")
axis(1, at = rows)
abline(v = 16, col = "grey85", lwd = 3)
abline(h = cut, lty = 2, col = "grey30")
for (k in names(series)) {
  v <- series[[k]]
  lines(rows, v, col = colours[[k]], lwd = 1.3)
  points(rows, v, pch = ifelse(v > cut, 16, 21), bg = "white", col = colours[[k]],
         cex = 1.1)
}
for (k in c(5, 7)) text(rows[k], series$default[k], sprintf("%.2f", series$default[k]),
                        adj = c(if (k == 5) 1.15 else -0.15, 1.5), cex = 0.72,
                        col = okabe[["blue"]])
text(16, par("usr")[3], "analytical\nmedial row", pos = 3, cex = 0.72, col = "grey40")
mtext(sprintf("threshold %.2f", cut), side = 4, at = cut, line = 0.3, cex = 0.72,
      col = "grey30")
text(16, series$default[6], "default", pos = 2, cex = 0.78, col = colours[["default"]],
     font = 2)
text(17, series$mlv2023[7], "mlv2023", pos = 4, cex = 0.78, col = colours[["mlv2023"]],
     font = 2)
par(op)
```

## Branch direction

A branch has no preferred direction, so its scores should not depend on the
end at which tracing started. Reversing every branch of the converging pair
and rescoring shows the difference between the two branch rules; only
`branch_rule` changes between the two rows:

```{r reversal}
reverse_all <- function(m) {
  m$branches <- lapply(m$branches, function(b) b[nrow(b):1, ])
  m
}
change <- function(m) {
  a <- compute_mat_properties(m, properties = P)$score_images
  b <- compute_mat_properties(reverse_all(m), properties = P)$score_images
  sapply(P, function(p) max(abs(a[[p]] - b[[p]]), na.rm = TRUE))
}
rbind(invariant = change(compute_mat(converging)),
      mlv2023 = change(compute_mat(converging, branch_rule = "mlv2023")))
```

The values are the largest change in any skeleton pixel's score. Under the
default rule they are zero. The `"mlv2023"` rule scores each point with forward
differences, so reversal changes parallelism, separation and taper
(MLV-M028); mirror changes only by rounding here because this axis is
straight and is fitted by one span in either direction.

## Where to go next

- `vignette("mlv-compatibility", package = "mlvtoolbox")`: reproducing
  published MLV values and choosing between the two modes.
- `feature_spec()` records every medial-axis setting so that a feature table
  can be rebuilt exactly; `analyse_mat(drawing, spec = spec)` applies it.
- `score_branch()` with `estimator = "arclength"` gives versions of the four
  scores defined by physical arc length, with windows and reference radii in
  pixels or degrees of visual angle.
